Madison County splits the work three ways. Land and buildings are valued by the Assessor of Property. Rates are voted by the County Commission and, inside Jackson, the City Council. The Trustee collects the county's bill. The Assessor has no say over the rate and collects nothing.

  • Trustee: courthouse first floor, 100 E. Main St., Suite 107, Jackson, TN 38301. Phone (731) 423-6027; hours 9:00 to 5:00 on weekdays.
  • Assessor of Property: third floor, Suite 304. Phone (731) 423-6063; hours 8:30 to 5:00 on weekdays.
  • City of Jackson Revenue Office: sends the city bill. Addresses inside Jackson owe the city as well as the county.

The county's Payment of Taxes page confirms that no payments or bills come from the Assessor. That office hands owner names and mailing addresses to the billing offices, so anyone who moves should update the address with the Assessor.

In West Tennessee, Madison County has Jackson as both seat and largest city. It counted 100,790 people on July 1, 2025, compared with 98,823 in the 2020 census. Of 44,744 housing units, 62.0% are owner-occupied. The middle owner-occupied house is valued at $211,800, rent in the middle is $1,123, and household income in the middle is $60,042.

Beyond Jackson, the county includes Medon, Three Way, Beech Bluff, Pinson and parts of Humboldt and Mercer, so check which taxing jurisdiction a parcel sits in before you quote a bill. Three Way and Humboldt, for example, can carry their own rates, and a rural address may be taxed by the county alone.

Reappraisal comes again in 2027, five years after 2022. Tennessee Code 67-5-1601 is why the county must keep to a schedule. Meanwhile the Assessor's staff walks roughly a third of all parcels each year, looking for changes to land or buildings.

An indicator on the Assessor's page puts the median residential sale price at $251,450 in January 2026, compared with $212,500 at the 2022 reappraisal, about 18.33% higher. That gap points to higher appraisals in 2027. Homes are assessed at 25 percent of appraised value, commercial property at 40 percent.

State law requires an Assessment Change Notice, mailed around May, to each owner whose value rose or fell. No notice means no change. Plenty of these are returned as undeliverable, so call the office if your address changed in the last two or three years.

Expect your notice in the first week of October; nothing can be paid ahead of that. To pay, search at paymadisontaxes.com, phone the Trustee on (731) 423-6027, or go to the courthouse. This office collects county property tax only, at the rate the County Commission sets.

The January 1 owner of record carries the year's tax, so a buyer who purchases mid-year will not appear on that bill. Figures printed on a closing statement are generally estimates, most of all before October 1, which is why the closing attorney is the person to ask who pays what. The Trustee can tell you the delinquency date and interest schedule.

If you are selling, plan the paperwork around that calendar. A house that closes in late summer will usually still be billed in the seller's name in October, so the closing attorney's estimate of the year's tax matters, and it helps to hand over a copy of the last bill so both sides work from the same figure.

Madison County property tax calendar
StepTiming
Assessment Change Notices mailedUsually May
Board of Equalization appointmentsLast two weeks of May
Board of Equalization hearingsWeekdays in the first two weeks of June
State Board filingAugust 1 or 45 days after the county notice, whichever is later
Tax notices arriveFirst week of October
Next reappraisal2027

Dial the Assessor at (731) 423-6063 and ask for the property record to be verified. Staff look over the property card, note your reasons and send a field appraiser to recheck. Should that fail to settle things, you move on to the Madison County Board of Equalization.

Five local property owners, drawn from the county and from Jackson, make up the board. State law has it hear appeals on weekdays in the first two weeks of June, and booking starts in the last two weeks of May. Check this year's dates with the Assessor. Only the current tax year is eligible; an appeal of 2025 taxes in 2026 is too late. While a case is open, keep paying the undisputed part so the account does not become delinquent.

A residential owner's file should hold comparable sales from one or two years before the tax year, a recent paid appraisal, and exterior and interior photos. Income-property owners need three years of leases, rent rolls, income and expense records, appraisals, sales contracts, closing statements and construction costs; withholding them can forfeit the chance to use them before the State Board. The appeal page adds that a State Board filing has a fee, of which $10 to $17 cannot be refunded, and that the undisputed tax must be paid before it turns delinquent. The State Board's number is 615-401-7883.

State relief applications are handled by the Trustee for elderly owners, disabled owners, disabled-veteran owners and surviving spouses of a disabled veteran. For current requirements, ring (731) 423-6027.

Pack a driver's license, Medicare card and Social Security card, together with income documents for yourself, your spouse and any other owner. For a mobile home, add a title copy or bill of sale. The dollar limits move yearly, so get the present income cap and deadline from the Trustee before deciding you qualify. Relief repays part of a bill you have already paid, so it lowers what you owe over time but does not remove the bill itself.

Before listing, request a written balance from the Trustee, and from the Jackson Revenue Office when the house is inside the city. Because the January 1 owner is named on the bill, that name stays even after a fall closing. Whether the buyer repays the seller for the months left in the year is worked out by the closing attorney on the statement.

Older balances, an estate to settle or an open appeal should be mentioned to the closing attorney before the contract date. Paying an old balance up front simplifies the file and avoids delay at the table. When a cash sale closes quickly, the sequence is the same: request the payoff, deduct it from proceeds, record the deed once taxes are clear. Bring the parcel number, the latest bill, and any notice about a value change so the closing attorney can see the whole picture in one pass.

faqs.q: Do I pay both the county and the city on a Jackson house?
faqs.a: Yes, for a house inside Jackson: county tax goes to the Trustee and city tax to the Revenue Office. Outside the city limits, only the county tax applies.

faqs.q: When is the next reappraisal in Madison County?
faqs.a: 2027. The previous one took effect in 2022, and a rise of about 18.33% in the median sale price since then suggests values will move.

faqs.q: Can I pay my Madison County taxes early?
faqs.a: No. Payment opens only after notices arrive, which should be the first week of October. If yours is missing, call the Trustee at (731) 423-6027.

faqs.q: Whose name is on the tax bill after I sell?
faqs.a: Probably the seller's. The January 1 owner stays on record for the whole year, and the closing attorney divides the cost between buyer and seller.

faqs.q: How long does the Board of Equalization meet?
faqs.a: Around two weeks, early in June, with weekday hearings and appointments taken in late May. Call (731) 423-6063 to confirm this year's schedule.
